sources.title: Environmental accounts on air emissions QMI

guard_patterns.handling: Require an ONS source row for each package.
Keep direct Scope 1 coverage explicit where applicable.
Keep SIC 2007 mapping and aggregation rules explicit.
Keep 2024 reference year and publication/revision dates explicit.
Keep MtCO2e, percentage, GVA and energy bases explicit.
Allow revisions and distinguish provisional from updated estimates.
Do not substitute territorial or consumption-footprint semantics for residence statistics.
Never infer parcel-level emissions from national environmental accounts.
Require explicit PASS review for every generated control.

packages.title: ONS residence-basis scope and geography boundary QA
facts: The 2024 Environmental Accounts measure UK greenhouse gas emissions on a residence basis.
Residence-basis emissions include UK residents and UK-registered businesses wherever they are in the world.
The ONS air-emissions geography is UK level rather than local-authority or parcel level.
Residence-basis estimates exclude emissions released in the UK by tourists and foreign transport operations.
Residence-basis estimates include emissions of UK residents abroad.
Businesses registered abroad but based in the UK are excluded from the residence measure.
Businesses registered in the UK but based abroad are included in the residence measure.
The residence basis differs from the territorial basis used by the NAEI starting inventory.
The residence boundary is required by the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting framework.
Residence statistics must not be treated as a direct measure of emissions occurring inside a specific UK parcel.

packages.title: ONS SEEA and National Accounts alignment QA
facts: UK Environmental Accounts follow the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting Central Framework.
The SEEA framework is aligned with the UN System of National Accounts.
The UK Environmental Accounts are aligned with the UK National Accounts.
This alignment supports comparison of environmental and economic statistics.
The residence principle allows greenhouse gas emissions to be linked to economic sectors.
Industry comparisons use Standard Industrial Classification 2007 codes.
The 2026 Environmental Accounts support comparisons at two-digit SIC level.
The air-emissions accounts are compiled annually by ONS with Ricardo Energy and Environment providing estimates.
SEEA consistency is intended to support international comparability.
Environmental Accounts should not be used as a substitute for territorial target-monitoring statistics such as net-zero progress.

packages.title: ONS NAEI source-to-SIC mapping QA
facts: The National Atmospheric Emissions Inventory is the main starting source for ONS air-emissions reporting.
NAEI emissions are calculated from activity data and emission factors.
The residence principle is applied after the territorial NAEI starting point.
NAEI source categories are not themselves based on SIC 2007 codes.
A mapping procedure is therefore required from NAEI sources to SIC 2007 industries.
Some NAEI sources map one-to-one to a single SIC code.
Other NAEI sources map one-to-many and must be split across several SIC codes.
One-to-many splits use direct or indirect information about proportional activity.
Motorway petrol consumption is an example of activity that can be distributed across many SIC sectors and households.
Gas oil used by freight trains is an example that can map one-to-one to the rail-transport SIC code.

packages.title: ONS direct Scope 1 residence-emissions QA
facts: ONS Air Emission Accounts include direct residence-based greenhouse gas emissions.
ONS describes these direct residence-based emissions as Scope 1 under greenhouse-gas protocol terminology.
The measure does not include emissions embedded in imported goods and services.
Because embedded imports are omitted, residence statistics are not a consumption-footprint measure.
The 2026 Environmental Accounts warn that these statistics cannot show emissions embedded in imports.
The 2026 Environmental Accounts warn against using them to draw conclusions on UK progress toward net-zero targets.
Household emissions in this framework are direct emissions attributed to consumer expenditure and household activities.
Industry emissions are attributed to the resident economic unit that directly emits them.
Scope 1 residence emissions can be compared with economic activity because of National Accounts alignment.
Scope 1 national accounts statistics must not be converted into Scope 2, Scope 3 or parcel-level values without separate evidence.

packages.title: ONS 2024 residence total and long-term trend QA
facts: ONS estimates 2024 UK residence-basis greenhouse gas emissions at 478 MtCO2e.
The 2024 residence total was 0.4% lower than 2023.
The 2024 total was the lowest since the current series began in 1990.
Residence-basis greenhouse gas emissions were 41.8% lower in 2024 than in 1990.
The long-run decline was mainly associated with a 67.4% fall in energy-industry emissions since 1990.
Households were the largest single contributor when compared with individual industries in 2024.
Households accounted for 25.9% of the 2024 residence total.
Industries collectively accounted for 74.1% of the 2024 residence total.
The transport industry was the largest emitting individual industry in 2024.
The 478 MtCO2e residence total must not be substituted for the lower territorial-emissions total.

packages.title: ONS household consumer-expenditure emissions QA
facts: Households accounted for 25.9% of UK residence-basis greenhouse gas emissions in 2024.
Households have been the largest single source category in this residence framework since 2015.
ONS assigns household emissions based on things individual consumers buy and use.
Household emissions also include activities where households act as employers.
An example of a household-as-employer activity is a family hiring a gardener.
Household emissions also include activities where households produce goods for their own use.
An example of own-use production is people growing vegetables for their own consumption.
Domestic travel, especially driving, is a main contributor to household emissions.
Heating homes is another main contributor to household emissions.
Travel and non-travel household emissions were at roughly similar levels by 2024, and together form consumer expenditure emissions.

packages.title: ONS transport and air-travel residence emissions QA
facts: Transport was the largest emitting individual industry in the 2024 residence accounts.
Transport industry emissions were estimated at 78 MtCO2e in 2024.
Transport accounted for 16.3% of total residence-basis emissions in 2024.
The transport industry includes taxis, underground rail, water transport and air travel.
Air transport accounted for 51.6% of transport-industry emissions in 2024.
Residence-basis air transport includes flights by UK-based airlines around the world.
Air-transport emissions fell by 58.1% in 2020 during pandemic travel restrictions.
In 2022, the first full year without those restrictions, air-transport emissions were 83.5% higher than in 2021.
Air-transport emissions were about 40 MtCO2e in 2024, more than double their 2020 level.
Residence-basis transport must not be confused with territorial domestic-transport definitions.

packages.title: ONS energy and manufacturing decline plus direct-energy mix QA
facts: Energy-industry residence emissions fell by 5.5% between 2023 and 2024.
The 2023-to-2024 energy-industry decline was smaller than the 13.7% decline between 2022 and 2023.
Manufacturing had the second-largest industry decrease in 2024, falling by 4.9%.
Energy-industry emissions were 67.4% lower in 2024 than in 1990.
UK direct energy use was 165.4 million tonnes of oil equivalent in 2024.
Fossil fuels accounted for 77.7% of direct energy use in 2024.
Natural gas accounted for 45.2% of fossil-fuel use, making it the largest single fossil source.
DERV road fuel and aviation fuel followed natural gas among major fossil-fuel sources.
Renewables increased from 0.8% of direct energy use in 1990 to 15.3% in 2024.
Wind, wave and tidal energy accounted for 28.4% of renewable energy use in 2024.

packages.title: ONS residence emissions-intensity and GVA QA
facts: Greenhouse gas emissions intensity is calculated as emissions per unit of economic output.
ONS calculates industry emissions intensity by dividing greenhouse gas emissions by gross value added.
GVA is output minus intermediate consumption for an industry.
The GVA series used is a chained-volume measure in constant prices with 2023 as the base year.
Consumer expenditure, often described as households, is excluded from emissions-intensity calculations.
UK emissions intensity was 140 tonnes CO2e per £1 million GVA in 2024.
There was no change in economy-wide emissions intensity between 2023 and 2024.
Emissions intensity fell by 72.0% between 1990 and 2024.
The series declined from 500 tonnes CO2e per £1 million GVA in 1990 to 140 in 2024.
Residence intensity omits emissions embedded in imports and therefore is not a full consumption-efficiency measure.

packages.title: ONS emissions-intensity revision and agriculture ranking QA
facts: ONS revised the emissions-intensity time series because of changes in how GVA is calculated.
Before the revision, the energy sector had been estimated as the most emissions-intensive sector.
After the revision, agriculture is estimated as the most emissions-intensive sector.
ONS states agriculture has consistently been the most emissions-intensive industry since 1990 under the revised series.
The GVA revision improved measurement of import and export prices for crude oil.
The GVA revision also improved measurement of natural-gas import and export prices.
The GVA revision also improved measurement of petroleum-product import and export prices.
Those changes revised energy-sector GVA upward.
A higher revised GVA changes calculated emissions intensity even if emissions themselves do not change by the same proportion.
Users must preserve the revised series and avoid mixing pre-revision intensity rankings with the current 2026 publication.

packages.title: ONS provisional versus updated industry-granularity QA
facts: ONS air-emissions estimates are published annually.
Ricardo delivers a provisional dataset at industry-section level before the more detailed update.
The provisional section-level release uses about 21 industry categories.
The updated release contains industry-group detail at roughly 130 categories.
Industry splits are based on SIC 2007.
Previously released datasets remain accessible to users.
The whole time series can be revised as methods improve or source data change.
ONS states that despite revisions the series is designed to remain comparable over time.
Current and provisional editions should not be combined without preserving their revision status and granularity.
A value from a provisional high-level section must not be presented as a final detailed SIC-group value.

packages.title: ONS aviation residence-adjustment methodology QA
facts: UNFCCC territorial reporting treats international aviation emissions as a memorandum item rather than part of national totals.
ONS Environmental Accounts include aviation on a residence basis.
Residence aviation includes take-off and landing emissions.
Residence aviation also includes greenhouse gas emissions during aircraft cruise.
The residence adjustment adds international-flight emissions from UK operators to and from the UK.
The adjustment subtracts corresponding emissions from foreign operators on international flights to and from the UK.
Civil Aviation Authority flight-kilometre data are used in the adjustment methodology.
Fuel-use information is available separately for domestic aviation, international aviation and military aviation.
Average fuel use per kilometre is calculated for the adjustment.
The residence aviation result should not be substituted for UNFCCC territorial aviation totals.

packages.title: ONS shipping bunker-fuel residence adjustment QA
facts: UNFCCC territorial reporting treats international shipping emissions as a memorandum item rather than part of national totals.
ONS Environmental Accounts make a residence adjustment for international shipping.
The adjustment adds fuel purchased overseas by UK operators.
The adjustment subtracts fuel purchased in the UK by foreign operators.
Fuel purchased in the UK by overseas operators is derived from total UK purchases minus estimated UK-operator purchases in the UK.
UK-operator purchases in the UK use balance-of-payments expenditure and a unit price per tonne from Quarterly Energy Prices.
Total UK fuel purchases used in the calculation are supplied from the national inventory through Ricardo Energy and Environment.
Fuel purchased overseas by UK operators is estimated from balance-of-payments bunker-fuel expenditure.
Average annual bunker prices are used to convert overseas expenditure to fuel volume.
Residence shipping emissions must not be mixed with territorial shipping memorandum-item treatment.

packages.title: ONS primary-emitter and ownership industry-allocation QA
facts: Environmental Accounts aim to allocate emissions to the industry that is the primary emitter and owns the emitting unit.
If a retailer owns trucks used to deliver stock, those truck emissions are allocated to the retail industry.
If the retailer hires a separate freight company, the truck emissions are allocated to the road-freight industry.
This ownership principle is part of converting activity-based inventory sources into economic-industry accounts.
NAEI sources can require splitting across several SIC divisions when the emitting activity is shared across the economy.
Motorway car activity is an example that can be distributed across industry, commerce, public administration and households.
National Travel Survey information can support the distribution of shared road activity.
Fuel-purchase information by industry can also support the allocation of shared road activity.
Some sources such as freight-train gas oil can map directly to a single SIC code.
Industry allocation in Environmental Accounts is an accounting classification and not evidence of parcel ownership or parcel emissions.

packages.title: ONS industry-allocation uncertainty and revision QA
facts: ONS publishes red-amber-green uncertainty ratings for the methodology used to allocate CO2, CH4 and N2O to industry groups.
Those ratings concern uncertainty in allocation to industry group.
Allocation uncertainty is additional to the underlying uncertainty in NAEI estimates.
The published allocation ratings do not include uncertainty introduced by residence adjustments.
One-to-many NAEI-to-SIC mappings are a source of allocation complexity.
Shared activities can require indirect proxies such as travel and purchase data.
Methodological improvements and supplier-data revisions can revise the historical time series.
ONS makes previous versions accessible so changes can be traced.
A revised time series should replace superseded values when reporting the current edition.
High-level national uncertainty evidence must not be converted into a parcel-specific confidence score without separate parcel evidence.
